# United States history

## 1776

**Declaration of Independence adopted**

On July 4, the Continental Congress adopted a declaration announcing that thirteen colonies were independent of Britain. Its statement of equality coexisted with slavery and the exclusion of many people from political rights.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1776_in_the_United_States&oldid=1363325998

## 1777

**Battle of the Assunpink Creek**

At Assunpink Creek near Trenton, George Washington's troops held off British attacks. The Americans then slipped away and won another engagement at Princeton, sustaining the revolutionary cause after earlier setbacks.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1777_in_the_United_States&oldid=1381575647

## 1778

**Treaty of Alliance (1778)**

France and the United States agreed to a military alliance during the Revolutionary War. French financial and military support, including naval assistance, became crucial to the American victory.

- France recognized and allied with the United States.
- The agreement expanded the war beyond Britain and its colonies.
- French support included money, troops, and naval power.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1778_in_the_United_States&oldid=1371257903

## 1779

**Battle of Kettle Creek**

Patriot militia defeated a Loyalist force at Kettle Creek in Georgia. The fighting illustrated the Revolution's bitter divisions within communities, especially in the southern colonies.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1779_in_the_United_States&oldid=1320574847

## 1780

**Siege of Charleston**

British forces captured Charleston, South Carolina, after a siege, taking thousands of American prisoners. The loss was a major setback for the Continental Army in the southern campaign.

.image image-0fc8dd75d33013bd.png 7 28

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1780_in_the_United_States&oldid=1379187135

: Original schematic illustration; not a historical photograph.

## 1781

**Battle of Cowpens**

At Cowpens, American forces under Daniel Morgan defeated a British force led by Banastre Tarleton. The victory weakened British operations in the South and helped set the stage for Yorktown.

- Daniel Morgan commanded the American force.
- Banastre Tarleton led the British troops.
- The victory strengthened the American position in the South.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1781_in_the_United_States&oldid=1278586867

## 1782

**Battle of Videau's Bridge**

Fighting continued in South Carolina even after the British surrender at Yorktown. At Videau's Bridge, American and British forces clashed during the war's closing months.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1782_in_the_United_States&oldid=1278586875

## 1783

**Treaty of Paris signed**

Britain and the United States signed the Treaty of Paris, ending the Revolutionary War. Britain recognized American independence and the agreement defined the new nation's boundaries.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1783_in_the_United_States&oldid=1332939563

## 1784

**Treaty of Paris ratified**

Congress ratified the Treaty of Paris, formally accepting the peace agreement with Britain. Ratification helped conclude the Revolution while many questions about the western borderlands remained contested.

- Congress approved the 1783 peace treaty.
- Britain had recognized American independence.
- Western boundaries remained a source of conflict.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1784_in_the_United_States&oldid=1327469979

## 1785

**Treaty of Fort McIntosh**

The United States negotiated the Treaty of Fort McIntosh with representatives of several Native nations. It sought land cessions and boundaries in the Ohio country, where American expansion continued to provoke conflict.

![Population context](parchment-chart:population-1785)

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1785_in_the_United_States&oldid=1278586902

: Chart context: OpenStax, U.S. History, United States Population Chart: https://openstax.org/books/us-history/pages/f-united-states-population-chart

: Population figures are historical context, not event counts; boundaries and census coverage changed. The 1780 figure is an estimate; the first census was in 1790.

## 1786

**Treaty of Hopewell**

The Treaty of Hopewell with the Choctaw was one of several agreements the United States made with southeastern Native nations. Such treaties defined claimed boundaries while settlers and federal officials continued to press for land.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1786_in_the_United_States&oldid=1328775185

## 1787

**United States Constitution signed**

Delegates meeting in Philadelphia signed a proposed Constitution to replace the Articles of Confederation. Its compromises created a stronger federal government while protecting slavery in several provisions.

- Delegates met in Philadelphia.
- The proposed Constitution strengthened federal institutions.
- Compromises in the text protected slavery.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1787_in_the_United_States&oldid=1369164627

## 1788

**United States Constitution ratified**

New Hampshire became the ninth state to ratify the Constitution, meeting the threshold for it to take effect. Ratification debates also produced demands for explicit protections of individual rights.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1788_in_the_United_States&oldid=1349991755

## 1789

**1788–89 United States presidential election**

George Washington was chosen as the first president under the Constitution, with John Adams as vice president. The new federal government began establishing institutions and precedents that would shape later administrations.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1789_in_the_United_States&oldid=1374568403

## 1790

**Compromise of 1790**

A political bargain linked federal assumption of state Revolutionary War debts to locating the permanent national capital on the Potomac. It reflected competing regional interests in the new republic.

- The federal government assumed state war debts.
- The permanent capital would be located on the Potomac.
- The bargain joined financial and regional interests.

.image image-f6b4aa9272d3dadd.png 7 28

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1790_in_the_United_States&oldid=1326580277

: Original schematic illustration; not a historical photograph.

## 1791

**Bill of Rights ratified**

The first ten amendments to the Constitution were ratified as the Bill of Rights. They protected freedoms such as speech and religion and established limits on federal power.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1791_in_the_United_States&oldid=1365260468

## 1792

**Postal Service Act**

The Postal Service Act strengthened the national postal system and provided for an expanding network of post roads. Newspapers received favorable treatment, helping information circulate across the growing republic.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1792_in_the_United_States&oldid=1374412712

## 1793

**Fugitive Slave Act of 1793**

Congress passed a law providing a federal process for enslavers to reclaim people who escaped across state lines. It reinforced slavery and threatened free Black people with kidnapping and wrongful seizure.

- The law provided a process for the return of escapees.
- It reinforced the system of slavery.
- Free Black people also faced the danger of wrongful seizure.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1793_in_the_United_States&oldid=1344430417

## 1794

**Whiskey Rebellion**

Resistance to a federal tax on distilled spirits culminated in the Whiskey Rebellion in western Pennsylvania. Washington mobilized militia, demonstrating the federal government's willingness to enforce its laws.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1794_in_the_United_States&oldid=1369765363

## 1795

**Naturalization Act of 1795**

The Naturalization Act increased the residency period required for citizenship and restricted eligibility to free white persons. It shaped an immigration system that explicitly excluded many people on racial grounds.

![Population context](parchment-chart:population-1795)

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1795_in_the_United_States&oldid=1337538997

: Chart context: OpenStax, U.S. History, United States Population Chart: https://openstax.org/books/us-history/pages/f-united-states-population-chart

: Population figures are historical context, not event counts; boundaries and census coverage changed. 

## 1796

**Jay Treaty**

Jay's Treaty with Britain took effect amid intense partisan controversy. It addressed unresolved disputes from the Revolution but disappointed Americans who wanted stronger concessions from Britain.

- The treaty addressed disputes with Britain.
- Supporters hoped to avoid war.
- Opponents criticized its concessions and terms.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1796_in_the_United_States&oldid=1384571906

## 1797

**Treaty of Tripoli**

The Senate approved a treaty intended to protect American shipping and secure peace with Tripoli. It was part of the young republic's efforts to negotiate with the Barbary states of North Africa.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1797_in_the_United_States&oldid=1386507396

## 1798

**Alien and Sedition Acts**

Congress passed the Alien and Sedition Acts during tensions with France. The laws expanded federal powers over immigrants and punished certain criticism of the government, provoking fierce opposition.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1798_in_the_United_States&oldid=1386508754

## 1799

**Logan Act**

The Logan Act sought to prevent unauthorized private citizens from negotiating with foreign governments over disputes with the United States. It arose amid partisan conflict over relations with France.

- The act targeted unauthorized private diplomacy.
- It arose from a dispute involving France.
- It reflected intense partisan tensions.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1799_in_the_United_States&oldid=1322978084

## 1800

**1800 United States presidential election**

Thomas Jefferson's victory over John Adams led to a transfer of power between rival political parties. A tie between Jefferson and Aaron Burr sent the final choice to the House of Representatives.

.image image-d256a678b02e6a1f.png 7 28

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1800_in_the_United_States&oldid=1385201133

: Original schematic illustration; not a historical photograph.

## 1801

**Contingent presidential election**

After repeated ballots, the House chose Thomas Jefferson over Aaron Burr as president. The electoral deadlock exposed flaws in the original presidential election system, later addressed by the Twelfth Amendment.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1801_in_the_United_States&oldid=1381514201

## 1802

**Judiciary Act of 1802**

Congress reorganized the federal judiciary and repealed a controversial law passed near the end of the Adams administration. The change formed part of a broader struggle between Federalists and Jeffersonian Republicans.

- Congress repealed an earlier judiciary law.
- The federal court system was reorganized.
- The dispute reflected a struggle between rival parties.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1802_in_the_United_States&oldid=1374598146

## 1803

**Louisiana Purchase**

The United States purchased Louisiana from France, vastly expanding the territory it claimed. The acquisition intensified questions about westward expansion, Indigenous sovereignty, and the future spread of slavery.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1803_in_the_United_States&oldid=1374598212

## 1804

**Lewis and Clark Expedition**

Meriwether Lewis and William Clark began their expedition up the Missouri River. Their journey gathered geographic and scientific information while depending on the knowledge and assistance of Native peoples.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1804_in_the_United_States&oldid=1374598285

## 1805

**Lewis and Clark reach the Pacific**

The Lewis and Clark expedition reached the Pacific coast after crossing the continent. The travelers spent the winter near the mouth of the Columbia River before beginning their return.

- The expedition crossed the continent.
- It reached the Pacific coast.
- The travelers wintered near the Columbia River.

![Population context](parchment-chart:population-1805)

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1805_in_the_United_States&oldid=1374598344

: Chart context: OpenStax, U.S. History, United States Population Chart: https://openstax.org/books/us-history/pages/f-united-states-population-chart

: Population figures are historical context, not event counts; boundaries and census coverage changed. 

## 1806

**Lewis and Clark return**

Lewis and Clark returned to St. Louis after their journey to the Pacific and back. Their reports informed American officials and settlers, though the lands they traversed were already home to many Native nations.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1806_in_the_United_States&oldid=1375051096

## 1807

**Act Prohibiting Importation of Slaves**

Congress prohibited the importation of enslaved people into the United States, effective in 1808. The law did not abolish slavery, and a large domestic trade in enslaved people continued.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1807_in_the_United_States&oldid=1375051117

## 1808

**1808 presidential election**

James Madison won the presidential election as a Democratic-Republican. He inherited tensions with Britain and France over maritime trade and American neutrality.

- James Madison won the presidency.
- He succeeded Thomas Jefferson.
- Foreign trade and neutrality remained pressing issues.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1808_in_the_United_States&oldid=1375051144

## 1809

**Non-Intercourse Act (1809)**

Congress replaced the broad embargo on overseas trade with restrictions directed at Britain and France. The measure sought to protect American interests without resolving the maritime disputes.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1809_in_the_United_States&oldid=1374598775

## 1810

**Macon's Bill No. 2**

Macon's Bill No. 2 reopened trade while offering to restore restrictions against either Britain or France if the other respected American shipping. The maneuver failed to prevent escalating conflict with Britain.

.image image-ddcce2cb62d7af8b.png 7 28

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1810_in_the_United_States&oldid=1371680018

: Original schematic illustration; not a historical photograph.

## 1811

**1811 German Coast Uprising**

Enslaved people rose against their enslavers along Louisiana's German Coast. Authorities and militias suppressed the uprising with deadly force, and participants faced executions and severe reprisals.

- Enslaved people organized the uprising in Louisiana.
- Militias and authorities suppressed the revolt.
- Participants faced executions and other reprisals.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1811_in_the_United_States&oldid=1369632421

## 1812

**War of 1812 begins**

The United States declared war on Britain after disputes over maritime rights and other tensions. The conflict was fought on land and water and involved Native nations as well as American and British forces.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1812_in_the_United_States&oldid=1374410006

## 1813

**Battle of Lake Erie**

An American naval force under Oliver Hazard Perry defeated a British squadron on Lake Erie. Control of the lake supported subsequent American operations in the Northwest.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1813_in_the_United_States&oldid=1368032457

## 1814

**battles of Emuckfaw and Enotachopo Creek**

Andrew Jackson's forces fought Red Stick Creek warriors at Emuckfaw and Enotachopo Creek in present-day Alabama. The battles formed part of the Creek War, which devastated Native communities and led to extensive land cessions.

- Andrew Jackson's forces fought Red Stick Creek warriors.
- The battles were part of the Creek War.
- The wider conflict brought devastating land losses.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1814_in_the_United_States&oldid=1383595243

## 1815

**Battle of New Orleans**

American forces defeated a British attack at New Orleans in January. The battle occurred after a peace treaty had been signed in Europe but before news of it reached the combatants.

![Population context](parchment-chart:population-1815)

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1815_in_the_United_States&oldid=1369628884

: Chart context: OpenStax, U.S. History, United States Population Chart: https://openstax.org/books/us-history/pages/f-united-states-population-chart

: Population figures are historical context, not event counts; boundaries and census coverage changed. 

## 1816

**Second Bank of the United States chartered**

Congress chartered the Second Bank of the United States to help manage federal finances and support a more stable currency. Arguments over its power later became central to national politics.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1816_in_the_United_States&oldid=1374265362

## 1817

**Rush–Bagot Treaty**

The Rush-Bagot agreement limited naval forces on the Great Lakes and Lake Champlain. It marked a step toward reducing tensions along the border between the United States and British North America.

- The agreement limited naval forces on shared waters.
- It applied to the Great Lakes and Lake Champlain.
- It reduced tensions with British North America.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1817_in_the_United_States&oldid=1369767099

## 1818

**Treaty of Tuscaloosa**

The Chickasaw agreed to cede a large area west of the Tennessee River in the Treaty of Tuscaloosa. The agreement opened land to American settlement at the expense of Indigenous control.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1818_in_the_United_States&oldid=1371406305

## 1819

**Tallmadge Amendment proposed**

Representative James Tallmadge proposed restricting slavery in Missouri as it sought statehood. The debate exposed deep sectional divisions over slavery's expansion.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1819_in_the_United_States&oldid=1369910265

## 1820

**Missouri Compromise**

The Missouri Compromise admitted Missouri as a slave state and Maine as a free state. It also drew a geographic line limiting slavery in much of the remaining Louisiana Purchase territory.

- Missouri entered as a slave state.
- Maine entered as a free state.
- A geographic line restricted slavery in much of the remaining Louisiana Purchase.

.image image-edd499aa9ff2be47.png 7 28

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1820_in_the_United_States&oldid=1374264782

: Original schematic illustration; not a historical photograph.

## 1821

**Missouri admitted as a state**

Missouri entered the Union as a slave state following the compromise over its admission. The controversy showed how adding states could upset the political balance between free and slave states.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1821_in_the_United_States&oldid=1369766679

## 1822

**United States House of Representatives elections, 1822**

Voters elected members of the House of Representatives during a period of shifting party alignments. The fading of the old Federalist Party preceded new divisions within national politics.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1822_in_the_United_States&oldid=1322982140

## 1823

**Monroe Doctrine announced**

President James Monroe warned European powers against further colonization or interference in the Americas. Later administrations invoked the Monroe Doctrine to justify a wider range of American policies.

- Monroe opposed further European colonization in the Americas.
- The statement also warned against European interference.
- Later administrations broadened its use.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1823_in_the_United_States&oldid=1372343455

## 1824

**1824 United States presidential election**

Four major candidates competed for the presidency, and no one won a majority of electoral votes. The resulting decision moved to the House of Representatives under the Twelfth Amendment.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1824_in_the_United_States&oldid=1381278889

## 1825

**House elects John Quincy Adams president**

The House elected John Quincy Adams president after the Electoral College produced no majority. Supporters of Andrew Jackson condemned the result, fueling political conflict in the following years.

![Population context](parchment-chart:population-1825)

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1825_in_the_United_States&oldid=1375226155

: Chart context: OpenStax, U.S. History, United States Population Chart: https://openstax.org/books/us-history/pages/f-united-states-population-chart

: Population figures are historical context, not event counts; boundaries and census coverage changed. 

## 1826

**Treaty of Washington (1826)**

A treaty signed in Washington revised an earlier agreement involving the Creek Nation and its lands in Georgia. The dispute reflected intense pressure on Native communities as the state sought their territory.

- The treaty revised an earlier agreement over Creek lands.
- Georgia pressed for access to the territory.
- Creek communities faced intense pressure and displacement.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1826_in_the_United_States&oldid=1380180354

## 1827

**Baltimore and Ohio Railroad chartered**

The Baltimore and Ohio Railroad received a charter to connect the port of Baltimore with inland markets. It became an early example of the railroad projects transforming American transportation.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1827_in_the_United_States&oldid=1370898325

## 1828

**Andrew Jackson elected president**

Andrew Jackson defeated John Quincy Adams in a fiercely contested presidential election. His campaign drew on an expanding electorate of white men while women and many others remained excluded.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1828_in_the_United_States&oldid=1374264789

## 1829

**Cincinnati riots of 1829**

Anti-Black violence in Cincinnati drove many Black residents from the city, with some resettling in Canada. The riots exposed the insecurity and discrimination faced by free Black communities in the North.

- White mobs attacked Black residents in Cincinnati.
- Many Black residents fled the city.
- Some sought a new home in Canada.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1829_in_the_United_States&oldid=1374381591

## 1830

**Indian Removal Act**

The Indian Removal Act authorized the federal government to negotiate exchanges of Native lands east of the Mississippi for lands farther west. Removal policies displaced Indigenous nations and caused immense suffering.

.image image-4e2b2e570a59cfb8.png 7 28

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1830_in_the_United_States&oldid=1374381533

: Original schematic illustration; not a historical photograph.

## 1831

**Nat Turner's Rebellion**

Nat Turner led an uprising of enslaved people in Virginia that killed dozens of white residents. Authorities suppressed the revolt and imposed harsher restrictions on enslaved and free Black people.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1831_in_the_United_States&oldid=1374381483

## 1832

**1832 Democratic National Convention**

Democrats held a national convention in Baltimore and nominated Martin Van Buren for vice president. The convention helped establish a party-nominating practice that became central to American elections.

- Democrats gathered in Baltimore.
- The convention nominated Martin Van Buren for vice president.
- National conventions became a lasting feature of party politics.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1832_in_the_United_States&oldid=1374381425

## 1833

**American Anti-Slavery Society founded**

Abolitionists founded the American Anti-Slavery Society to campaign for the immediate end of slavery. Black and white activists organized meetings, petitions, and publications despite intense resistance.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1833_in_the_United_States&oldid=1374381374

## 1834

**Indian Trade and Intercourse Act**

Congress revised federal rules governing trade and relations with Native nations. The law operated within a policy framework that increasingly pushed Indigenous peoples away from their homelands.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1834_in_the_United_States&oldid=1374381330

## 1835

**Battle of Gonzales**

Texian settlers resisted Mexican troops at Gonzales, beginning open fighting in the Texas Revolution. The conflict grew from disputes over governance, settlement, and slavery.

- Texian settlers resisted a Mexican force at Gonzales.
- The confrontation began open fighting in the Texas Revolution.
- Disputes involved settlement, political authority, and slavery.

![Population context](parchment-chart:population-1835)

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1835_in_the_United_States&oldid=1374381263

: Chart context: OpenStax, U.S. History, United States Population Chart: https://openstax.org/books/us-history/pages/f-united-states-population-chart

: Population figures are historical context, not event counts; boundaries and census coverage changed. 

## 1836

**Battle of the Alamo**

Mexican forces captured the Alamo after a siege, killing its defenders. The battle became a rallying point for Texian forces, which later defeated Mexico at San Jacinto.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1836_in_the_United_States&oldid=1374381224

## 1837

**Panic of 1837**

A financial panic triggered bank failures, unemployment, and a prolonged downturn. The crisis followed land speculation and disputes over banking and federal monetary policy.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1837_in_the_United_States&oldid=1369753804

## 1838

**United States Exploring Expedition**

The United States Exploring Expedition departed on a long voyage of scientific exploration and surveying. Its crews collected specimens and mapped Pacific waters, contributing to American scientific institutions.

- The expedition sailed from the United States.
- Its crews surveyed and mapped Pacific waters.
- They collected specimens for scientific study.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1838_in_the_United_States&oldid=1358511107

## 1839

**Mississippi permits married women to own property**

Mississippi enacted a law allowing married women to hold certain property in their own names. Its protections were limited, and the law also reflected the slaveholding economy of the state.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1839_in_the_United_States&oldid=1369652934

## 1840

**1840 United States presidential election**

William Henry Harrison defeated Martin Van Buren in an election marked by mass campaigning and the log-cabin image. The Whigs blamed the incumbent administration for economic hardship.

.image image-e91d3ebd770e0d24.png 7 28

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1840_in_the_United_States&oldid=1385825022

: Original schematic illustration; not a historical photograph.

## 1841

**President William Henry Harrison dies**

William Henry Harrison died shortly after taking office, and Vice President John Tyler assumed the presidency. Tyler's succession established an important precedent for presidential transitions.

- Harrison died soon after taking office.
- Vice President John Tyler became president.
- The succession established a precedent for later transitions.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1841_in_the_United_States&oldid=1372328435

## 1842

**Dorr Rebellion**

In Rhode Island, competing governments emerged from a dispute over voting rights and the state's restrictive charter. The Dorr Rebellion highlighted growing demands to expand political participation.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1842_in_the_United_States&oldid=1369649163

## 1843

**Great Migration on the Oregon Trail**

A large group of emigrants traveled west on the Oregon Trail. Their journey accelerated settlement by Americans in a region already inhabited and governed by Indigenous peoples.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1843_in_the_United_States&oldid=1332607829

## 1844

**Great Flood of 1844**

Severe flooding affected the Missouri and Mississippi river systems, damaging farms and settlements. The disaster demonstrated the vulnerability of growing communities along major waterways.

- Flooding affected the Missouri and Mississippi river systems.
- Farms and settlements suffered damage.
- River communities faced major transportation disruptions.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1844_in_the_United_States&oldid=1374095154

## 1845

**Texas annexed by the United States**

The United States annexed Texas, which had been an independent republic after breaking from Mexico. The move intensified a boundary dispute with Mexico and the national conflict over slavery's expansion.

![Population context](parchment-chart:population-1845)

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1845_in_the_United_States&oldid=1329996053

: Population figures are historical context, not event counts; boundaries and census coverage changed. 

## 1846

**Battle of Palo Alto**

American and Mexican forces fought at Palo Alto near the Rio Grande. The battle was an early engagement in the Mexican-American War, which reshaped the continent's political boundaries.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1846_in_the_United_States&oldid=1369806087

## 1847

- A stricter fugitive slave law strengthened enforcement.

Representative Preston Brooks attacked Senator Charles Sumner on the Senate floor after Sumner condemned slavery and its supporters. The assault dramatized the escalating violence of sectional politics.

John Brown and his followers raided the federal armory at Harpers Ferry, hoping to help spark an uprising against slavery. The raid failed, and Brown's execution intensified sectional tensions.

**Oklahoma City bombing**

A truck bomb destroyed much of the Alfred P. Murrah Federal Building in Oklahoma City. The domestic terrorist attack killed 168 people, including children in a day care center.

![Population context](parchment-chart:population-1995)

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1995_in_the_United_States&oldid=1386910000

: Chart context: OpenStax, U.S. History, United States Population Chart: https://openstax.org/books/us-history/pages/f-united-states-population-chart

: Population figures are historical context, not event counts; boundaries and census coverage changed. 

## 1996

**Line Item Veto Act of 1996**

The Line Item Veto Act gave the president authority to cancel certain spending and tax provisions. The Supreme Court struck down the law in 1998 as inconsistent with the Constitution's lawmaking process.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1996_in_the_United_States&oldid=1385794213

## 1997

**Mars Pathfinder landing**

NASA's Mars Pathfinder landed on Mars and deployed the small Sojourner rover. Images and scientific measurements demonstrated a relatively low-cost approach to planetary exploration.

- Pathfinder landed on Mars.
- It deployed the Sojourner rover.
- The mission returned images and scientific measurements.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1997_in_the_United_States&oldid=1384030394

## 1998

**Bill Clinton impeached**

The House of Representatives impeached President Bill Clinton on charges arising from the Lewinsky investigation. The Senate acquitted him in the trial held the following year.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1998_in_the_United_States&oldid=1386433016

## 1999

**Columbine High School massacre**

Two students attacked Columbine High School in Colorado, killing students and a teacher before taking their own lives. The shooting intensified national debate about school safety and gun violence.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1999_in_the_United_States&oldid=1386631072

## 2000

**2000 presidential election**

George W. Bush won the presidency after a disputed Florida vote and a Supreme Court decision affecting the recount. The close result renewed debate about election administration and the Electoral College.

- Florida's vote became the focus of a recount dispute.
- A Supreme Court decision affected the recount.
- George W. Bush won the Electoral College.

.image image-64b0f69bfb511f2d.png 7 28

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2000_in_the_United_States&oldid=1383836065

: Original schematic illustration; not a historical photograph.

## 2001

**September 11 attacks**

Al-Qaeda hijackers attacked the World Trade Center and the Pentagon; another hijacked plane crashed in Pennsylvania. The attacks killed nearly 3,000 people and reshaped American security and foreign policy.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2001_in_the_United_States&oldid=1384636284

## 2002

**No Child Left Behind Act**

The No Child Left Behind Act expanded federal requirements for testing and school accountability. Supporters sought to close achievement gaps, while critics challenged its testing and funding approach.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2002_in_the_United_States&oldid=1385603816

## 2003

**Space Shuttle Columbia disaster**

Space Shuttle Columbia broke apart during reentry, killing all seven astronauts aboard. The investigation identified damage sustained during launch and broader failures in safety culture.

- Columbia broke apart during reentry.
- All seven astronauts aboard were killed.
- Investigators examined launch damage and safety culture.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2003_in_the_United_States&oldid=1379126582

## 2004

**George W. Bush reelected**

George W. Bush won reelection over John Kerry. The wars in Iraq and Afghanistan, national security, and domestic policy featured prominently in the campaign.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2004_in_the_United_States&oldid=1386846331

## 2005

**Hurricane Katrina**

Hurricane Katrina devastated the Gulf Coast, and levee failures caused catastrophic flooding in New Orleans. The disaster exposed failures in emergency response and deep inequalities in vulnerability and recovery.

![Population context](parchment-chart:population-2005)

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2005_in_the_United_States&oldid=1385428462

: Chart context: OpenStax, U.S. History, United States Population Chart: https://openstax.org/books/us-history/pages/f-united-states-population-chart

: Population figures are historical context, not event counts; boundaries and census coverage changed. 

## 2006

**Sago Mine disaster**

An explosion at the Sago Mine in West Virginia trapped coal miners underground. Twelve miners died, and the disaster prompted renewed attention to mine safety and rescue procedures.

- An explosion trapped miners at Sago.
- Twelve miners died.
- The disaster renewed attention to mine rescue and safety.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2006_in_the_United_States&oldid=1384311498

## 2007

**Virginia Tech shooting**

A gunman killed students and faculty at Virginia Tech before taking his own life. The tragedy intensified debate about campus safety, mental health, and access to firearms.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2007_in_the_United_States&oldid=1386771701

## 2008

**Barack Obama elected president**

Barack Obama won the presidential election, becoming the first Black president-elect of the United States. His campaign unfolded amid the financial crisis and a severe economic downturn.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2008_in_the_United_States&oldid=1386482447

## 2009

**Barack Obama inaugurated**

Barack Obama was inaugurated as the forty-fourth president. His administration took office during a financial crisis, wars overseas, and rising unemployment.

- Obama became the forty-fourth president.
- He took office during a financial crisis.
- Unemployment and overseas wars were major challenges.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2009_in_the_United_States&oldid=1386846449

## 2010

**Affordable Care Act signed**

President Obama signed the Affordable Care Act, expanding health insurance coverage and changing insurance rules. The law remained the subject of political and legal disputes.

.image image-6de5a34542a4a6ce.png 7 28

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2010_in_the_United_States&oldid=1382224014

: Original schematic illustration; not a historical photograph.

## 2011

**Osama bin Laden killed**

United States forces killed al-Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden during a raid in Pakistan. He had been a central figure in planning the September 11 attacks.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2011_in_the_United_States&oldid=1386873684

## 2012

**Hurricane Sandy**

Hurricane Sandy caused widespread flooding and damage across the northeastern United States. Its storm surge severely affected New York and New Jersey and disrupted infrastructure.

- Sandy struck the northeastern United States.
- Storm surge flooded coastal communities.
- Infrastructure and transportation were disrupted.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2012_in_the_United_States&oldid=1386792890

## 2013

**Boston Marathon bombing**

Bombs exploded near the finish line of the Boston Marathon, killing and injuring spectators. The attack prompted an extensive investigation and a regional manhunt.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2013_in_the_United_States&oldid=1386581290

## 2014

**Ferguson protests**

Protests followed the police killing of Michael Brown in Ferguson, Missouri. The demonstrations drew national attention to police practices, racial inequality, and accountability.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2014_in_the_United_States&oldid=1386793006

## 2015

**Obergefell v. Hodges**

In Obergefell v. Hodges, the Supreme Court held that same-sex couples have a constitutional right to marry. The decision required states to license and recognize those marriages.

- The Supreme Court recognized a right to same-sex marriage.
- States were required to license qualifying marriages.
- States also had to recognize such marriages from elsewhere.

![Population context](parchment-chart:population-2015)

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2015_in_the_United_States&oldid=1386202195

: Chart context: OpenStax, U.S. History, United States Population Chart: https://openstax.org/books/us-history/pages/f-united-states-population-chart

: Population figures are historical context, not event counts; boundaries and census coverage changed. 

## 2016

**Donald Trump elected president**

Donald Trump won the presidency in the Electoral College while Hillary Clinton received more votes nationwide. The election exposed deep divisions over economic policy, immigration, and political institutions.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2016_in_the_United_States&oldid=1386891533

## 2017

**Women's March**

The Women's March brought large crowds to Washington and many other cities after Donald Trump's inauguration. Participants advocated a range of causes, including women's rights and opposition to administration policies.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2017_in_the_United_States&oldid=1386847352

## 2018

**Parkland school shooting**

A gunman attacked Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland, Florida, killing students and staff. Survivors organized nationally for changes to gun laws and school safety.

- The attack occurred at a high school in Parkland, Florida.
- Students and staff were killed.
- Survivors organized for changes to gun policy.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2018_in_the_United_States&oldid=1386847470

## 2019

**Donald Trump impeached**

The House of Representatives impeached President Donald Trump over his dealings with Ukraine. The Senate acquitted him in the trial held in 2020.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2019_in_the_United_States&oldid=1386501478

## 2020

**COVID-19 pandemic**

COVID-19 spread across the United States, causing widespread illness and death. Public health measures, economic disruption, and disagreements over the response affected daily life nationwide.

.image image-65e6dbd54d1577ee.png 7 28

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2020_in_the_United_States&oldid=1386793501

: Original schematic illustration; not a historical photograph.

## 2021

**January 6 Capitol attack**

A crowd of Donald Trump supporters attacked the United States Capitol as Congress met to count electoral votes. The attack disrupted the proceedings, which later resumed.

- Supporters of Donald Trump entered the Capitol.
- Congress was counting electoral votes.
- The count resumed after the disruption.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2021_in_the_United_States&oldid=1386952200

## 2022

**Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization**

In Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization, the Supreme Court overruled Roe v. Wade. The ruling returned much abortion regulation to elected officials, resulting in sharply different state laws.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2022_in_the_United_States&oldid=1386505204

## 2023

**Donald Trump indicted**

Donald Trump was indicted in several criminal cases, including a New York case involving business records. The prosecutions raised unprecedented questions about a former president facing criminal charges.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2023_in_the_United_States&oldid=1386847712

## 2024

**Donald Trump elected president**

Donald Trump won the presidential election, defeating Kamala Harris. His victory returned him to the White House after a four-year interval between terms.

- Donald Trump defeated Kamala Harris.
- He won a second presidential term.
- The election returned him to office after a four-year interval.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2024_in_the_United_States&oldid=1386182126

## 2025

**Donald Trump inaugurated**

Donald Trump was inaugurated for a second, nonconsecutive presidential term. The transition brought changes in federal leadership and policy priorities.

![Population context](parchment-chart:population-2025)

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2025_in_the_United_States&oldid=1383825058

: Chart context: OpenStax, U.S. History, United States Population Chart: https://openstax.org/books/us-history/pages/f-united-states-population-chart

: Population figures are historical context, not event counts; boundaries and census coverage changed. 

## 2026

**United States Semiquincentennial**

The United States marked 250 years since the Declaration of Independence. The semiquincentennial invited communities to consider both the nation's founding principles and the history of people excluded from them.

: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2026_in_the_United_States&oldid=1386915278
